q2: SELECT ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID FROM ( SELECT COUNT(*) CNT,ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID FROM ACTORDIRECTOR GROUP BY ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID HAVING CNT >= 3 ) FYI
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID FROM ACTORDIRECTOR GROUP BY ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID HAVING COUNT(*)>=3
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID FROM ( SELECT COUNT(*) CNT,ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID FROM ACTORDIRECTOR GROUP BY ACTOR_ID,DIRECTOR_ID HAVING CNT >= 3 ) FYI
counterexample: INSERT INTO ACTORDIRECTOR (TIMESTAMP, ACTOR_ID, DIRECTOR_ID) VALUES (1, 1, 1), (2, 1, 1), (3, 1, 1), (4, 2, 2), (5, 2, 2), (6, 3, 3);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 directly groups by ACTOR_ID and DIRECTOR_ID and applies the HAVING clause on the count of rows, while Q2 first groups by ACTOR_ID and DIRECTOR_ID, counts the rows, and then groups by the count (CNT) and the original ACTOR_ID and DIRECTOR_ID, applying the HAVING clause on the count. This difference in grouping and the application of the HAVING clause can lead to different results.
counterexample_dsp: The difference is triggered when there are multiple rows with the same ACTOR_ID and DIRECTOR_ID, and the count of such rows is not a distinct value. In this case, Q1 will return the ACTOR_ID and DIRECTOR_ID, while Q2 will not, because Q2 groups by the count (CNT) and the original ACTOR_ID and DIRECTOR_ID, and the count is not a distinct value.
